newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Belarus scientists to test forest cleanup plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Belarus scientists to test forest cleanup plan.

text.p: U.S. and Belarus researchers plan to test a way to clean up forests in Belarus contaminated 10 years ago by the world's worst nuclear accident at Chernobyl, U.S. scientists said on Wednesday.

The researchers and an American company will work on the plan to build a pilot biomass-fired power plant in Belarus that will burn contaminated wood and litter from the forest floor and turn it into electrical energy.
Radioactive elements, mainly cesium and strontium, would be captured in the ash and could then be disposed of as low-level or very low-level waste, the researchers said.
The $1.6 million plan was announced by Sandia National Laboratories, a U.S. Department of Energy facility in Livermore, 40 miles (65 kms) east of San Francisco.
"Because of the humanitarian aspect, I think it's the most exciting project I've ever worked on," said Larry Baxter, a chemical engineer at Sandia National Laboratories.
Construction of the pilot plant in Belarus is scheduled to start in April next year and become operational a year after that, he said.

The project will evaluate health, environmental and economic consequences of the pilot plant, designed to burn timber harbouring almost all the radioactive residue and capture radioactivity in the ash.
If successful, "the next step would be to build quite a number of commercial-scale facilities," Baxter said.

The pilot plant is expected to burn about two tons (2.032 tonnes) of material a day, compared with the 2,000 tons (2,032 tonnes) of plant matter burned each day at a commercial plant operating in California.
Belarus, which lies to the north of Chernobyl in neighbouring Ukraine, received about 70 percent of the radioactive fallout released during the Chernobyl explosion and fires.
The accident spewed an estimated 200 times the radiation unleashed by the atomic bombs that were dropped on Nagasaki and Hiroshima, Baxter said.

About a quarter of the total area of Belarus was severely contaminated by the April 26, 1986, accident. Contamination is concentrated mainly in the heavily forested southeastern portion of the country, researchers said.

Left alone, the contaminated regions would take hundreds of years to return to acceptable levels of radioactivity, Baxter said. If the plan succeeds, that process could be cut to between 30 and 40 years, he said.

It woould also reduce health risks to humans posed by ingesting the radioactive nuclides. Although it is prohibited, some residents enter the contaminated forests to gather food and collect firewood, Baxter said.
A second benefit of the project could be to reduce Belarus's heavy dependence on imported energy.

Baxter and researchers at the Institute of Power Engineering Problems, which was part of the Soviet Academy of Sciences under the former Soviet Union, will join with Wheelabrator Environmental Systems Inc, a division of Wheelabrator Technologies Inc of Hampton, New Hampshire, to build the pilot plant.

Wheelabrator, which operates five biomass and 16 trash-to-energy plants, is contributing half of the $1.6 million expense for the two-year project. The remaining half was split equally between Sandia National Laboratories and Belarus.
